title: SpaceX Lists on Thursday at $1.77 Trillion. It Will Instantly Be the Ninth Most Valuable Company on Earth.
excerpt: The largest IPO in history prices at $135 per share, raising $75 billion. Included in the package: Elon Musk's AI company xAI, Starlink's 7,000-satellite network, and a $41 billion accumulated deficit.
body:
On Thursday, June 12, SpaceX will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX. The company has set a fixed price of $135 per share and plans to sell 555,555,555 shares, raising approximately $75 billion. At that price, SpaceX will carry a market capitalisation of $1.77 trillion, making it instantly the ninth most valuable public company in the world — larger than Berkshire Hathaway, larger than Broadcom, and roughly equal to the combined market value of Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and every other publicly traded aerospace company on the planet.

It will be the largest initial public offering in American history, more than tripling Alibaba's $25 billion record from 2014.

## What You Are Actually Buying

SpaceX is no longer just a rocket company. The entity going public is a conglomerate that now includes three distinct businesses.

First, the launch business. SpaceX conducted a record number of Falcon 9 launches in 2025 and is developing Starship, the fully reusable super-heavy launch vehicle that the company considers essential to scaling every other part of its operations. Starship development alone consumed over $15 billion in capital expenditure last year.

Second, Starlink. The satellite internet constellation now has roughly 7,000 satellites in orbit and provides broadband service across more than 80 countries. Revenue from Starlink has been growing rapidly and represents the majority of SpaceX's $18.7 billion in 2025 revenue. SpaceX claims a total addressable market of $1.6 trillion for connectivity solutions — a figure that Morningstar analyst Nicolas Owens disputes, noting that it "equates to essentially every dollar spent on mobile services on Earth."

Third, xAI. Earlier this year, Elon Musk merged his artificial intelligence company into SpaceX. The S-1 filing allocates $12.7 billion of total 2025 capital expenditure to AI infrastructure initiatives. SpaceX's prospectus claims a $26.5 trillion total addressable market from AI — a number that, by any measure, is aspirational.

## The Numbers That Should Give You Pause

At $1.77 trillion, SpaceX trades at roughly 95 times its trailing revenue — nearly five times the ratio commanded by Nvidia, the most expensive of the Magnificent Seven stocks. The company posted a $4.9 billion net loss in 2025 and another $4.27 billion in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Its accumulated deficit — the total lifetime losses the company has not yet earned back — stands at $41.3 billion.

Capital expenditure exceeded revenue in 2025, with SpaceX spending $20.7 billion while earning $18.7 billion. The S-1 filing reveals that part of the IPO proceeds may be used to repay a $20 billion bridge loan that refinanced debt associated with X (formerly Twitter) and xAI. That bridge loan may need to be repaid within six months of the IPO.

Morningstar values SpaceX at approximately $780 billion — less than half the IPO price.

## Why Indian Investors Are Paying Attention

For the millions of Indian investors and NRIs with exposure to US markets — whether through direct brokerage accounts, exchange-traded funds, or India-listed international fund-of-funds — the SpaceX IPO will have immediate consequences.

The Nasdaq has already changed its rules to allow SpaceX inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 index as soon as 15 days after listing. That means anyone holding a QQQ or similar Nasdaq-100 ETF could have automatic exposure to SpaceX within weeks. The S&P 500, however, has declined to fast-track inclusion, requiring at least a year of trading and consistent profitability.

CNBC's Jim Cramer has warned that the sheer size of the offering could pull capital away from existing technology giants. Investors who want to buy SpaceX may sell holdings in Amazon, Microsoft, and Nvidia to fund their positions — a rotation that would ripple through every portfolio with US tech exposure.

There is also Starlink's India story. SpaceX has been seeking regulatory approval for satellite broadband services in India for years, competing with Mukesh Ambani's Jio for spectrum access. A public listing strengthens Starlink's case for Indian market entry and gives it the capital to compete.

## The Bigger Picture

SpaceX is listing during a week when global markets are already strained. Oil prices have surged past $96 on fresh Iran-Israel hostilities. The European Central Bank is expected to raise rates on Thursday. The Federal Reserve has signalled it may hike rates later this year after a stronger-than-expected jobs report.

Into this turbulence comes a company asking public investors to fund the next phase of a capital programme that spans rocket launches, satellite networks, AI data centres, and orbital infrastructure — all while carrying $41 billion in accumulated losses.

The company is, by any conventional metric, spectacularly overpriced. It is also, by any measure of ambition, unlike anything the public markets have seen before. That tension — between the financials as they are and the future as SpaceX imagines it — will define the most consequential IPO of the decade.
